topic: Ulcerative Colitis Toxic Megacolon Emergent Subtotal Colectomy
stem: A 32-year-old woman with a 4-year history of ulcerative colitis is hospitalized with an acute severe flare. Despite 4 days of intensive intravenous methylprednisolone (60 mg daily), she deteriorates acutely. Over the past 12 hours, her frequent bloody diarrhea abruptly decreases from 10 stools/day to zero stools, accompanied by progressive abdominal distension, severe nausea, and obstipation. On physical examination, she appears toxic, pale, and lethargic. Vital signs: temperature 39.2 C (102.6 F), blood pressure 84/52 mm Hg, heart rate 134/min, and respirations 26/min. Abdominal examination reveals severe tympanitic abdominal distension with diffuse rebound tenderness, involuntary muscular guarding, and absent bowel sounds (diffuse peritonitis). Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: white blood cell count 26,400/mm3 with 24% band forms, hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, serum potassium 3.1 mEq/L, and serum lactate 4.2 mmol/L. An urgent portable abdominal radiograph demonstrates marked, non-obstructive dilation of the transverse colon measuring 7.8 cm in diameter (abnormal threshold > 6.0 cm) with loss of normal colonic haustral markings ('lead-pipe' appearance) and mucosal pseudopolyps, with no free subdiaphragmatic air. The patient fulfills Jalan criteria for TOXIC MEGACOLON complicated by septic shock and peritonitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in definitive management?

options.text: Emergent surgical intervention with subtotal colectomy and end ileostomy (with preservation of the rectum), combined with aggressive fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
options.explanation: TOXIC MEGACOLON IN INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE (JALAN CRITERIA AND SURGICAL MANAGEMENT): (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Severe transmural inflammation extends deep into the circular and longitudinal smooth muscle layers of the colon. Massive local nitric oxide synthesis and tissue necrosis paralyze the neuromuscular apparatus of the colon, abolishing smooth muscle tone. As motility ceases, the colon dilates rapidly, producing a thin, friable, paper-like colonic wall susceptible to micro-perforation, bacterial translocation, and catastrophic free perforation; (2) DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (JALAN CRITERIA): Requires RADIOGRAPHIC EVIDENCE OF COLONIC DILATION (TRANSVERSE COLON DIAMETER > 6.0 CM ON PLAIN FILM OR CT) PLUS AT LEAST THREE OF THE FOLLOWING SYSTEMIC SIGNS: (a) Fever > 38.6 C; (b) Tachycardia > 120/min; (c) Leukocytosis > 10,500/mm3; (d) Anemia; PLUS AT LEAST ONE SIGN OF TOXICITY (hypotension, altered sensorium, electrolyte derangement, or dehydration). (3) CLINICAL PITFALL: An abrupt CESSATION OF DIARRHEA in severe colitis is an alarming sign of colonic atony and impending perforation, NOT clinical recovery; (4) SURGICAL MANAGEMENT OF CHOICE: In patients with toxic megacolon who present with PERITONITIS, PERFORATION, REFRACTORY SEPTIC SHOCK, OR WHO FAIL MEDICAL THERAPY WITHIN 24 TO 72 HOURS, EMERGENT SURGICAL RESECTION IS LIFE-SAVING. THE OPERATION OF CHOICE IS: SUBTOTAL COLECTOMY WITH END ILEOSTOMY (and Hartmann closure or mucous fistula of the rectal stump): (a) Removes the entire diseased, necrotic colonic source of sepsis; (b) Avoids entering the deep pelvis in an acutely septic, malnourished patient; (c) Preserves the rectum and anal sphincter complex for a future elective restoration of intestinal continuity (ileal pouch-anal anastomosis [IPAA]) once the patient has fully recovered; (5) CONTRAINDICATIONS: Colonoscopy and barium enemas are STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED because insufflation of air or contrast into a paper-thin toxic colon causes immediate catastrophic free perforation.

options.text: Perform an emergent colonoscopy with decompression tube placement to evacuate colonic gas
options.explanation: Colonoscopy with air insufflation in toxic megacolon is strictly contraindicated; mechanical distension causes immediate transmural colonic perforation, fecal peritonitis, and death.

options.text: Administer an urgent barium contrast enema to assess the mucosal lining of the colon
options.explanation: Barium contrast enemas in toxic megacolon cause catastrophic colonic perforation and lethal barium peritonitis; they are absolutely contraindicated.

options.text: Switch intravenous methylprednisolone to oral mesalamine 4 g daily and observe for 5 days
options.explanation: 5-ASA agents (mesalamine) are completely useless in toxic megacolon and delay necessary surgical resection; peritonitis and shock require immediate operative source control.

options.text: Perform an emergent one-stage total proctocolectomy with immediate ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA)
options.explanation: Pelvic dissection and immediate pouch construction in an unstable patient in septic shock on high-dose steroids carries prohibitive rates of anastomotic breakdown, pelvic sepsis, and death; subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy is standard.

topic: Subclinical Hypothyroidism Watchful Waiting vs Treatment Criteria
stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic for a routine health maintenance visit. She feels generally well and denies cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain, dry skin, hair thinning, menstrual abnormalities, or depressed mood. She is postmenopausal and has no history of cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or osteoporosis. Her only medication is a daily multivitamin. Physical examination reveals normal vital signs: blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, heart rate 72/min, and BMI 24.1 kg/m2. Examination of the neck demonstrates a normal-sized, non-tender thyroid gland with no palpable nodules. Deep tendon reflexes have a normal relaxation phase. Routine screening laboratory evaluation demonstrates: serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) mildly elevated at 6.8 mIU/L (reference range 0.4-4.2 mIU/L), with a completely normal serum free thyroxine (free T4) of 1.3 ng/dL (reference range 0.8-1.8 ng/dL). Repeat laboratory testing performed 8 weeks later confirms persistent mild TSH elevation at 6.9 mIU/L with normal free T4 (1.2 ng/dL). Serum anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies are negative (< 10 IU/mL; normal < 35 IU/mL). The patient asks whether she should start taking daily thyroid hormone pills. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan according to American Thyroid Association (ATA) and European Thyroid Association (ETA) guidelines?

options.text: Initiation of daily oral levothyroxine 100 mcg to suppress TSH below 1.0 mIU/L
options.explanation: Starting high-dose levothyroxine for mild asymptomatic SCH causes iatrogenic subclinical thyrotoxicosis, precipitating atrial fibrillation, osteoporosis, and increased cardiovascular mortality.

options.text: Observation and watchful waiting with repeat serum TSH and free T4 in 6 to 12 months, withholding levothyroxine therapy, as routine treatment is not recommended for asymptomatic mild TSH elevation (TSH < 10 mIU/L) with negative antibodies in non-pregnant adults
options.explanation: SUBCLINICAL HYPOTHYROIDISM (SCH) CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES (ATA 2014 / ETA GUIDELINES): (1) DEFINITION: Elevated serum TSH (above laboratory reference range) with a normal circulating free T4 concentration. Classified into two categories: (a) Grade 1 (mild): TSH between 4.5 and 9.9 mIU/L (accounts for > 75% of cases); (b) Grade 2 (severe): TSH >= 10.0 mIU/L; (2) NATURAL HISTORY OF MILD SUBCLINICAL HYPOTHYROIDISM: Transient TSH elevations occur frequently (e.g., recovery from viral illness, assay fluctuations). In patients with confirmed Grade 1 SCH (TSH 5-10 mIU/L) and NEGATIVE ANTI-TPO ANTIBODIES, spontaneous reversion to normal euthyroid TSH occurs in up to 50% to 60% of patients over 1 to 5 years, and progression to overt hypothyroidism is very low (~2% per year); (3) EVIDENCE FROM RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIALS (THE TRUST TRIAL, Stott et al., NEJM 2017): The Thyroid Hormone Replacement for Subclinical Hypothyroidism Trial (TRUST) randomized 737 older adults with subclinical hypothyroidism to levothyroxine vs placebo. RESULTS: Levothyroxine provided ZERO IMPROVEMENT in hypothyroid symptoms, tiredness score, quality of life, cognitive function, or muscle strength compared to placebo; (4) GUIDELINE CRITERIA FOR INITIATING LEVOTHYROXINE IN SCH: Treatment is DEFINITIVELY RECOMMENDED ONLY in: (a) SEVERE TSH ELEVATION: TSH >= 10.0 mIU/L; (b) PREGNANCY OR WOMEN ACTIVELY PLANNING PREGNANCY; (c) Presence of a symptomatic goiter or high anti-TPO antibody titers; (d) Severe clinical symptoms in a younger patient. In this 52-year-old asymptomatic woman with TSH 6.9 mIU/L, negative anti-TPO antibodies, and normal free T4, LEVOTHYROXINE IS NOT RECOMMENDED; periodic annual monitoring is the evidence-based standard of care.

options.text: Initiation of combination therapy with oral levothyroxine (T4) and liothyronine (T3)
options.explanation: Combination T3/T4 therapy has no proven benefit over levothyroxine monotherapy and is completely inappropriate in a patient who has no indication for thyroid hormone therapy in the first place.

options.text: Perform an emergent radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) scan to evaluate thyroid function
options.explanation: Radioiodine uptake scans are indicated for hyperthyroidism (suppressed TSH) to differentiate Graves disease from toxic adenomas; in elevated TSH, RAIU is useless and contraindicated.

options.text: Initiate daily oral potassium iodide supplements to enhance thyroid hormone synthesis
options.explanation: Exogenous iodide supplementation can induce profound, permanent hypothyroidism via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect; it is completely contraindicated.

stem: A 56-year-old man with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis and chronic ascites presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of worsening abdominal distension, mild diffuse abdominal discomfort, and low-grade fever. He denies hematemesis, melena, or diarrhea. On physical examination, he appears chronically ill, jaundiced, and mildly lethargic (asterixis is present). Vital signs: temperature 38.1 C (100.6 F), blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg, heart rate 94/min, and respirations 18/min. Abdominal examination demonstrates shifting dullness consistent with large ascites and mild diffuse tenderness to palpation without rebound tenderness or involuntary guarding. Bedside diagnostic paracentesis is performed immediately: ascitic fluid is cloudy yellow, and laboratory analysis reveals: white blood cell count 1,200/microL with 78% polymorphonuclear leukocytes (absolute neutrophil count [ANC] = 1,200 x 0.78 = 936/microL; diagnostic threshold >= 250/microL), total protein 0.9 g/dL, and glucose 68 mg/dL. Ascitic fluid Gram stain shows no organisms seen, and fluid is inoculated directly into blood culture bottles at the bedside. Serum laboratory evaluation reveals: BUN 34 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.7 mg/dL (baseline was 0.9 mg/dL 1 month ago, indicating acute kidney injury), total bilirubin 5.4 mg/dL, and prothrombin time/INR 1.9. The patient fulfills criteria for SPONTANEOUS BACTERIAL PERITONITIS (SBP). Which of the following represents the most appropriate, evidence-based pharmacological regimen to treat the infection and prevent hepatorenal syndrome according to American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) guidelines?

options.text: Monotherapy with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily, withholding all intravenous albumin to avoid volume overload
options.explanation: Omitting intravenous albumin in SBP with renal impairment (creatinine 1.7, BUN 34) triples the incidence of hepatorenal syndrome and increases mortality from 10% to 29% (Sort trial); albumin is mandatory.

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days as primary initial inpatient therapy
options.explanation: Oral fluoroquinolones are inadequate for acute inpatient SBP with renal dysfunction and encephalopathy, and high fluoroquinolone resistance exists; intravenous third-generation cephalosporins are first-line.

options.text: Intravenous administration of a third-generation cephalosporin (such as cefotaxime 2 g every 8 hours or ceftriaxone 2 g daily) COMBINED WITH intravenous albumin infusion (1.5 g/kg within 6 hours of diagnosis, followed by 1.0 g/kg on day 3)
options.explanation: SPONTANEOUS BACTERIAL PERITONITIS (SBP) AND ADJUNCTIVE ALBUMIN (AASLD GUIDELINES): (1) DEFINITION AND DIAGNOSIS: Bacterial infection of ascitic fluid without an identifiable surgically treatable intra-abdominal source. DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA: ASCITIC FLUID ABSOLUTE NEUTROPHIL COUNT (ANC) >= 250 CELLS/MICROL (0.25 x 10^9/L). Treatment must be initiated immediately upon finding ANC >= 250, without waiting for culture results; (2) EMPIRIC ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY: INTRAVENOUS THIRD-GENERATION CEPHALOSPORINS (CEFOTAXIME 2 G Q8H OR CEFTRIAXONE 2 G DAILY) are the gold-standard first-line agents. Third-generation cephalosporins achieve high concentrations in ascitic fluid and cover the predominant causal organisms: aerobic Gram-negative bacilli (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae) and non-enterococcal streptococci; (3) DECISIVE ROLE OF INTRAVENOUS ALBUMIN (THE SORT TRIAL): SBP triggers massive systemic and splanchnic vasodilation, precipitating acute circulatory dysfunction and HEPATORENAL SYNDROME (HRS), which is the leading cause of death in SBP (> 30% of patients develop renal failure). LANDMARK CLINICAL TRIAL EVIDENCE (Sort et al., NEJM 1999): Adding INTRAVENOUS ALBUMIN (1.5 G/KG WITHIN 6 HOURS OF DIAGNOSIS, FOLLOWED BY 1.0 G/KG ON DAY 3) to antibiotic therapy resulted in: (a) A DRAMATIC REDUCTION IN RENAL IMPAIRMENT FROM 33% TO 10% (p = 0.002); (b) A SIGNIFICANT REDUCTION IN IN-HOSPITAL MORTALITY FROM 29% TO 10% (p = 0.01). (Albumin expands effective arterial blood volume, scavenges nitric oxide, and suppresses compensatory renal vasoconstriction); (4) AASLD CRITERIA FOR ALBUMIN: Albumin is strongly indicated for all patients with SBP, especially those with renal impairment (creatinine > 1.0 mg/dL, BUN > 30 mg/dL) or severe liver failure (bilirubin > 4.0 mg/dL); (5) SECONDARY PROPHYLAXIS: Long-term daily oral ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin must be initiated upon completion of treatment.

options.text: Emergent exploratory laparotomy to inspect for occult bowel perforation
options.explanation: Unnecessary surgical exploration in cirrhotic patients with SBP carries an operative mortality > 50-80%; secondary peritonitis is ruled out by low protein (< 1 g) and response to medical therapy.

options.text: Administration of broad-spectrum intravenous vancomycin, cefepime, and metronidazole without albumin
options.explanation: Routine ultra-broad anaerobic coverage is unnecessary for classic community-acquired SBP and omits essential life-saving albumin, causing fatal hepatorenal syndrome.

topic: Acute Otitis Media First-Line Antimicrobial Selection and Amoxicillin Dosing
stem: A 20-month-old previously healthy boy is brought to the pediatric urgent care clinic by his mother because of a 2-day history of high fever, acute fussiness, poor sleeping, and constant tugging at his right ear. He has had mild clear rhinorrhea for 4 days. He attends a daycare center. His medical history is notable for one prior episode of acute otitis media at 11 months of age, which was treated successfully with amoxicillin. He has not received any antibiotics within the past 6 months. He has no known drug allergies. On physical examination, the child is irritable and crying. Vital signs: temperature 39.2 C (102.6 F), blood pressure 92/58 mm Hg, heart rate 132/min, and respirations 24/min. Otoscopic examination of the right ear reveals a markedly bulging, opaque, erythematous tympanic membrane with distinctly diminished mobility on pneumatic otoscopy, purulent middle ear effusion, and obscured landmarks. The left tympanic membrane is translucent and mobile with normal light reflex. Examination of the conjunctivae reveals clear sclerae without erythema or purulent exudate. Throat examination reveals mild pharyngeal erythema without tonsillar exudate. Which of the following represents the most appropriate, guideline-directed first-line antimicrobial regimen and dosage according to American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidelines?

options.text: Oral standard-dose amoxicillin (40 mg/kg/day divided into three doses daily) for 10 days
options.explanation: Standard-dose amoxicillin achieves inadequate middle ear fluid concentrations against penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae with mutated PBPs; high-dose amoxicillin (80-90 mg/kg/day) is mandatory.

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (90 mg/kg/day) as standard first-line therapy for all initial episodes of acute otitis media
options.explanation: Routine upfront amoxicillin-clavulanate causes high rates of gastrointestinal diarrhea and clavulanate-induced adverse events; it is reserved for patients with prior amoxicillin within 30 days or concurrent purulent conjunctivitis.

options.text: Oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg on day 1 followed by 5 mg/kg daily for 4 days
options.explanation: Macrolides have unacceptably high pneumococcal resistance (> 30-40%) and poor middle ear bactericidal eradication; azithromycin is reserved only for severe Type I IgE-mediated penicillin anaphylaxis.

options.text: Oral high-dose amoxicillin (80 to 90 mg/kg/day divided into two doses daily) for 10 days
options.explanation: PEDIATRIC ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA (AOM) ANTIMICROBIAL SELECTION (AAP GUIDELINES): (1) DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA: Requires moderate-to-severe bulging of the tympanic membrane OR new-onset otorrhea not due to otitis externa, OR mild bulging with intense erythema or ear pain; (2) MICROBIOLOGY: The predominant bacterial pathogens are: (a) STREPTOCOCCUS PNEUMONIAE (~35-40%); (b) NON-TYPEABLE HAEMOPHILUS INFLUENZAE (~30-35%); (c) MORAXELLA CATARRHALIS (~10-15%); (3) FIRST-LINE ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN: ORAL HIGH-DOSE AMOXICILLIN (80 TO 90 MG/KG/DAY IN 2 DIVIDED DOSES). Rationale for high dose: Penicillin resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae is mediated by ALTERATIONS IN PENICILLIN-BINDING PROTEINS (PBPs), NOT beta-lactamase production. High-dose amoxicillin achieves high middle ear fluid concentrations (>= 2-4 mcg/mL) that overcome low- and intermediate-affinity mutated PBPs, eradicating > 90-95% of penicillin-resistant pneumococci. Standard-dose amoxicillin (40 mg/kg/day) fails against resistant S. pneumoniae; (4) INDICATIONS FOR STEPPING UP TO AMOXICILLIN-CLAVULANATE (AUGMENTIN): Amoxicillin-clavulanate (90 mg/kg/day amoxicillin with 6.4 mg/kg/day clavulanate in a 14:1 ratio) is indicated FIRST-LINE ONLY IF: (a) Patient received amoxicillin in the PRECEDING 30 DAYS (high likelihood of beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae or M. catarrhalis); (b) CONCURRENT PURULENT CONJUNCTIVITIS ('otitis-conjunctivitis syndrome', predominantly caused by beta-lactamase-producing non-typeable H. influenzae); (c) Failure to respond to high-dose amoxicillin after 48 to 72 hours; (5) DURATION: Children < 2 years old require a FULL 10-DAY COURSE to minimize clinical relapse and persistent effusion.

options.text: Withhold all antibiotics and initiate watchful waiting without antimicrobial therapy for 48 hours
options.explanation: Watchful waiting without antibiotics is appropriate only for unilateral, non-severe AOM in children >= 2 years old without severe pain; in an infant < 2 years old with high fever (39.2 C) and severe bulging, immediate antibiotic therapy is required.

subject: Ethics
topic: Clinical Research Ethics Therapeutic Misconception and Vulnerable Populations
stem: A 64-year-old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer that has progressed through two lines of systemic chemotherapy and immunotherapy is evaluated by an oncologist regarding participation in a Phase I first-in-human clinical trial evaluating an experimental novel monoclonal antibody. The oncologist spends 45 minutes thoroughly reviewing the formal institutional review board (IRB)-approved consent document. The oncologist explicitly details that this is a dose-escalation phase I safety and toxicity study designed primarily to determine the maximum tolerated dose, pharmacokinetic clearance, and dose-limiting toxicities in humans, with an unknown and very low probability of direct therapeutic tumor shrinkage. All known potential adverse risks are described in detail. The patient listens attentively, nods, and signs the consent form. However, at the conclusion of the interview, the patient smiles warmly and says to the research nurse: 'I am so grateful to doctor for enrolling me in this new program. I know that standard chemotherapy failed, but this new trial treatment is my cure. I know that doctor chose this medicine specifically because it will cure my cancer and save my life.' Which of the following ethical phenomena does the patient's statement exemplify, and what is the primary ethical obligation of the research team?

options.text: The patient is expressing realistic therapeutic hope, and the research team should immediately administer the investigational drug without further discussion
options.explanation: The patient stated that the trial was chosen specifically to cure his cancer and save his life; this is an explicit therapeutic misconception that invalidates informed consent; proceeding without clarification violates research ethics.

options.text: The patient is demonstrating severe cognitive incompetence, requiring an immediate petition to state court for involuntary psychiatric guardianship
options.explanation: Expressing therapeutic misconception is an informational misunderstanding, not legal incompetence or psychosis; court guardianship is completely inappropriate.

options.text: The research team should immediately withdraw the patient from the trial permanently, as expressing optimism disqualifies subjects from Phase I research
options.explanation: Optimism and hope do not disqualify patients; the ethical duty is to educate and correct the misconception so the patient can make an authentic, informed choice.

options.text: The research team should modify the Phase I trial protocol to guarantee personalized therapeutic dosing for this individual patient
options.explanation: Investigators cannot unilaterally alter scientific trial protocols to provide personalized therapy; doing so destroys scientific validity and violates IRB approval.

options.text: The patient is demonstrating the 'Therapeutic Misconception,' and the research team is ethically obligated to pause the enrollment process, clarify the distinction between research protocols and personalized medical therapy, and ensure authentic understanding before proceeding
options.explanation: RESEARCH ETHICS AND THE THERAPEUTIC MISCONCEPTION (THE BELMONT REPORT AND DECLARATION OF HELSINKI): (1) DEFINITION OF THE THERAPEUTIC MISCONCEPTION: The therapeutic misconception occurs when a research subject conflates the fundamental purpose of CLINICAL RESEARCH (which is to generate generalizable scientific knowledge for future patients) with the purpose of CLINICAL MEDICAL CARE (which is to provide individualized diagnosis and therapy tailored specifically to benefit the individual patient). Patients harboring the therapeutic misconception mistakenly believe that every aspect of the research trial has been designed for their personal therapeutic benefit and that the investigator will personalize dosing or interventions to cure their disease; (2) FREQUENCY AND CONSEQUENCES: Extremely common in early-phase oncology trials (affecting > 50% to 70% of participants in Phase I studies). While patients may realistically maintain 'therapeutic hope,' the therapeutic misconception invalidates the foundational ethical requirement of INFORMED CONSENT: consent is not truly informed if the subject fundamentally misunderstands the purpose, nature, and risks/benefits of the trial; (3) ETHICAL OBLIGATIONS OF THE INVESTIGATOR AND STUDY TEAM: (a) MANDATORY RE-EDUCATION AND CLARIFICATION: The research team cannot simply accept a signed consent document when an explicit therapeutic misconception has been verbalized; (b) THE TEAM MUST PAUSE ENROLLMENT: Explicitly clarify that Phase I trials are safety/toxicity studies, explain that the drug is unproven, and reiterate that the investigator cannot adjust procedures purely for individualized benefit; (c) ASSESS COMPREHENSION: Re-evaluate the subject's comprehension before administering any investigational agent; (4) VULNERABLE POPULATIONS: Terminally ill patients facing refractory cancer are vulnerable to therapeutic misconception due to existential distress and desperation, requiring heightened scrutiny by Institutional Review Boards (IRBs).
